questions.text: Complete the table below, showing the Lewis structure and shape for IF5 and BrF4-.
questions.expectedAnswer: IF5: Lewis structure shows Br central atom with 5 bonding pairs to F atoms and 1 lone pair. Shape: square pyramidal. BrF4-: I central atom with 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs. Shape: square planar.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: TWO correct Lewis structures with shapes.

questions.text:
The reaction between boron trifluoride, BF3(g), and hydrogen, H2(g), is explosive:

2BF3(g) + 3H2(g) -> 6HF(g) + N2(g)

Calculate DrH for the reaction, given:

N2H4(l) + 2F2(g) -> N2(g) + 4HF(g)   DrH = -1094 kJ mol-1
BF3(g) + 3/2H2(g) -> NH3(g) + 3/2F2(g)   DrH = +260 kJ mol-1
N2H4(l) + H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)   DrH = -188 kJ mol-1
questions.expectedAnswer: Using Hess's law: manipulate and combine the given equations to get the target equation. DrH = -1866 kJ mol-1 (accept variations depending on manipulation).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises need to manipulate equations. Merit: Correct process with one error. Excellence: Correct answer with units.

questions.text:
Justify, in terms of the entropy changes of the system and the surroundings, why the reaction between BF3 and H2 is spontaneous.

2BF3(g) + 3H2(g) -> 6HF(g) + N2(g)
questions.expectedAnswer: The reaction is highly exothermic, so heat released to surroundings increases their entropy (positive dS_surr). The system goes from 5 moles of gas to 7 moles, increasing disorder (positive dS_sys). Both contributions make dS_total positive, so the reaction is spontaneous.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises entropy is positive. Merit: Explains entropy for system and surroundings. Excellence: Fully justifies spontaneity.

questions.text:
The table gives electron configurations of three elements.

Xenon, Xe: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p6
Xeypton, Xe: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6
Selenium, Se: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4

When considering the 3p4 part of the electron configuration of sulfur, what is represented by:
3
p
4
questions.expectedAnswer: 3 = the third energy level/shell. p = the p subshell/orbital type. 4 = the number of electrons in this subshell.

questions.text: Krrange Xe, Kr, and S in order of decreasing first ionisation energy. Justify your order using periodic trends.
questions.expectedAnswer: Order: Kr > S > Xe (approximately). Kr has the highest IE because it has a full outer shell (stable configuration). S has a lower IE than Kr because it has fewer protons for the same shell. Xe has lower IE than Kr because it has more electron shells (greater shielding/distance).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises one factor. Merit: Explains with two factors. Excellence: Justifies for all three.

questions.text:
The two possible shapes of bromine trifluoride, BrF3, are T-shaped and trigonal planar. Both are based on trigonal bipyramidal electron arrangement.

Research shows BrF3 is polar.

Compare the two shapes to identify which would result in a polar molecule.

Refer to bond polarity and arrangement of bond dipoles.
questions.expectedAnswer: In trigonal planar, the 3 Cl-F dipoles cancel symmetrically. In T-shaped (with 2 lone pairs in equatorial positions), the dipoles do NOT cancel, giving a net dipole. Since BrF3 is polar, it must be T-shaped.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies polarity of each shape. Merit: Compares using dipole arrangement. Excellence: Full explanation with lone pair positions.

questions.text:
Identify all types of attractive forces between particles of these substances in their liquid state.

Ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2 (bp 17 degrees C)
Hydrogen bromide, HBr (bp -67 degrees C)
Pentane, C5H12 (bp 36 degrees C)
questions.expectedAnswer: CH3NH2: Hydrogen bonding, permanent dipole-dipole, London dispersion forces. HCl: Permanent dipole-dipole, London dispersion forces. Butane: London dispersion forces only.

questions.text: Explain the difference in the boiling points of ethylamine and hydrogen chloride.
questions.expectedAnswer: Despite HCl being more polarisable, CH3NH2 has hydrogen bonding (H bonded to N) which is stronger than the dipole-dipole forces in HCl. However, HCl has a much lower bp because it lacks H-bonding and has weaker overall forces.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises H-bonding is stronger. Merit: Explains why ethylamine has higher bp.

questions.text: Explain why the boiling point of butane is higher than that of hydrogen chloride.
questions.expectedAnswer: Butane has only London dispersion forces, but it has a much larger molecular size with more electrons, giving stronger LDF than the weaker forces in the smaller HCl molecule.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises size/electron cloud. Merit: Explains chain length gives stronger forces. Excellence: Compares all three.

questions.text:
The enthalpy of combustion of ethanol, C2H5OH, was determined experimentally. The ethanol was combusted to heat water.

Data: initial water temp = 20.5 degrees C, final = 28.7 degrees C, initial mass of burner and ethanol = 58.2 g, final = 57.6 g.

The student calculated DcH(C2H5OH(l)) = -726 kJ mol-1.
Specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g-1 degC-1.
M(C2H5OH) = 32.0 g mol-1

Calculate the mass of the water in the beaker.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: One step correct. Merit: Correct process with one error. Excellence: Correct mass.

questions.text:
Which quantity would have been a source of error in the calculated enthalpy value?

    temperature change of water          mass of fuel combusted

Explain your choice.
questions.expectedAnswer: Temperature change of water. Heat is lost to the surroundings (beaker, air) so the measured temperature change is less than the actual heat produced. This makes the calculated enthalpy less exothermic than the true value.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies temperature change and ONE reason. Merit: Explains ONE reason for the error.
